artifact.output:
Read this before deploy, not after

Four constraints that were found, not anticipated

Each one is measured. Each one fails quietly. If this service is about to become load-bearing for anyone other than you, these are the things that will bite, in the order they will bite.

The short version

  1. One replica. Not two. Replay protection doesn't degrade under scale-out — it stops working.
  2. Long polls die near 100s behind Cloudflare. Keep MAX_AWAIT_MS under whatever your proxy allows.
  3. Serve the client from /mcp, not /mcp.js. A CDN may cache by extension whatever your headers say.
  4. Participant links are capabilities, not identities. This is not an audit trail. Don't deploy expecting one.
Constraint 01

Run exactly one replica

The replay-protection nonce store is in memory (src/adapters/crypto/nonces.ts). Every signed request carries a nonce that is accepted once, which is what stops a captured request being replayed inside its five-minute freshness window.

What actually happens with two replicas

A nonce burned on replica A is unknown to replica B. A replayed request routed to B succeeds. Replay protection does not degrade under horizontal scaling; it stops working — silently, and only for the requests that happen to land on the wrong pod.

The Deployment therefore pins replicas: 1 with a Recreate strategy. This is the single most important operational constraint in the system.

What to do

Leave replicas: 1 alone. Scaling out is possible, but it means moving the nonce store to Postgres or Redis first.

Treat the replica count and the nonce store as one change, never two. The moment replicas changes, that is the thing that has to change with it.

Constraint 02

Long polls die at about 100 seconds behind Cloudflare

Cloudflare gives an origin roughly 100 seconds to respond before it answers 524 itself.

Measured through the tunnel

A 150-second poll died at 125 seconds with HTTP 524 and no body. Not a slow response — no response, and no way for the caller to tell a dead wait from an empty one.

Holding a connection past that ceiling does not make the caller wait longer; it makes the wait fail. MAX_AWAIT_MS therefore defaults to 90 seconds: every poll returns inside the window, and one that exhausts its budget comes back with timedOut: true plus whatever has arrived so far. A timeout is a legitimate outcome, not an error. The MCP client loops shorter polls, so a caller asking for five minutes still gets five minutes.

What to do

If you deploy behind something other than Cloudflare, find that proxy's own timeout and set MAX_AWAIT_MS below it.

Whatever sits in front of this service decides the real ceiling. The service only decides whether it respects it.

Constraint 03

A CDN may cache by file extension regardless of what you send

/mcp.js was served with cache-control: no-store and came back from the edge with cf-cache-status: HIT and an injected max-age=14400. Cloudflare caches .js by default, by extension, whatever the origin intended.

The visible symptom

For four hours after every deploy, agents installed the previous client. Nothing errored. Everything worked — one deploy behind.

The fix is in the path, not in the headers. The canonical URL for the MCP client is /mcp, with no extension. /mcp.js remains as an alias for anyone who saved the old URL.

What to do

Hand out /mcp. Never /mcp.js.

If you put any CDN in front of this, check what it caches by default. Origin headers are a request, not an instruction — and this failure mode is silent.

Constraint 04

Participant links are capabilities

Anyone holding a participant link can answer as that participant. A forwarded link is a forwarded identity.

This is deliberate, and it is the reason the product works at all: participants need no account, no email verification, and no Claude access. Attribution is whichever link was used — which costs nothing and is honest about what it is.

The limit, stated plainly

It is not an audit trail. Do not deploy this expecting one. If responses ever need to be contested, that is the point to add verified identity — and that is a change to this service, not a configuration option waiting to be switched on.

What you do control is the window. LINK_TTL_HOURS bounds how long a link stays answerable, and expiry is checked inside the query that resolves a token rather than after it. The schema also carries revoked_at and honours it on every resolve — but nothing exposes revocation over HTTP yet.

What to do

Set LINK_TTL_HOURS deliberately before you send the first link out. It is your only real control.

Killing one link today is an update against participant_links. Make sure whoever is on call knows that, and has the access to do it.

Pre-deploy checklist

  • replicas: 1 confirmed in the Deployment, with strategy Recreate.
  • Nobody has an autoscaler, HPA, or "just bump it for the launch" plan pointed at this service.
  • MAX_AWAIT_MS is set below the timeout of whatever proxy is actually in front of you.
  • Proxy timeout verified by measurement, not by documentation.
  • Install instructions, READMEs, and onboarding docs all point at /mcp.
  • CDN default caching rules reviewed for any path this service serves.
  • LINK_TTL_HOURS chosen on purpose and agreed with whoever owns the risk.
  • Everyone consuming this understands that link attribution is not an audit trail.
  • At least one on-call person has database access to revoke a link manually.
Source: docs/SELF-HOSTING.md — "Constraints that are measured, not theoretical."

scenarios.title: What the first self-hosting attempt exposed

artifact.output:
Three things self-hosting exposed

Each one presented as a symptom that pointed somewhere other than its cause. If you are standing up your own deployment, you will probably hit at least one of them. Here is what you will see, and where to actually look.

OneEvery MCP call returns unauthorized

Symptom Every single call fails with unauthorized. Not the first one, not intermittently — all of them.

Points at Signing. A bad key, a clock skew, a header the server stopped accepting.

Actually is The client is talking to the wrong host.

The MCP client shipped with this deployment's own URL hardcoded as the default base URL. If you self-hosted and then followed /start by hand, you installed a client that pointed at somebody else's host — and signed its requests with a key that host had never issued and could not possibly recognise.

From the client's side that is indistinguishable from a broken signature. The request is well-formed, the key is real, the rejection is total. Nothing in the error names an address, so nothing tells you the address is the problem. You will spend the afternoon re-issuing keys.

The fix, and how to confirm it

The instance now substitutes its own URL into the client file when it serves it — the same way /cli already worked. A client downloaded from your deployment talks to your deployment.

If you have an older copy on disk, check it before you debug anything else:

grep -n 'baseUrl\|BASE_URL' path/to/mcp.js

If the host in there is not yours, that is the whole bug. Re-download from your own instance rather than editing it in place, so you also pick up anything else that changed.

The generalisation: a default that is correct for exactly one deployment is a landmine for every other one. Any constant that names a host belongs in the response body at serve time, not in the file in the repository.

TwoThe claude mcp add command on /start arrives as one line

Symptom You copy the multi-line install command off /start and it pastes as a single joined line, with the shell-continuation backslashes gone.

Points at Clipboard handling, the copy button, whitespace collapsing in the browser, the <pre> styling.

Actually is A lone trailing backslash inside a JavaScript template literal.

Inside a template literal, a backslash at the end of a line is a line continuation. It does not produce a backslash character. It removes itself and the newline that follows it, and it does so silently — no warning, no error, nothing at runtime to notice.

// What you wrote:
const cmd = `claude mcp add sirdocalot \
  --transport http \
  --url ${url}`;

// What the string actually contains:
"claude mcp add sirdocalot   --transport http   --url https://..."

So the page is faithfully rendering exactly what it was given. The copy button is fine. The clipboard is fine. The backslashes were eaten before the HTML existed.

The fix

Escape the backslash so it survives the literal:

const cmd = `claude mcp add sirdocalot \\
  --transport http \\
  --url ${url}`;

The generalisation: when generated output is missing a character that shell syntax also treats as special, suspect the generator's own escaping before you suspect the transport. Template literals and shell scripts both claim the backslash, and the template literal gets it first.

ThreeMAX_AWAIT_MS=90s quietly becomes 90 milliseconds' worth of nothing

Symptom A timeout you configured has no effect. Behaviour matches the default exactly, as if your environment variable were never set.

Points at The variable not reaching the process — wrong .env file, wrong service unit, wrong container layer, a typo in the name.

Actually is The value reached the process, failed to parse, and was replaced with the default without a word.

Writing MAX_AWAIT_MS=90s is a natural mistake — the unit is right there in the name, so appending it feels like clarification. It parses as NaN. The loader fell back to its default and carried on.

That is the sharp edge: this happened in a loader whose entire stated posture is refusing loudly. Every other class of misconfiguration in it stops the process with a message. This one class — a value present but unparseable as a number — slipped through to a silent default, which is the single behaviour the loader exists to prevent. A silent fallback is worse than an absent variable, because an absent variable at least leaves you looking in the right place.

The fix

The loader refuses now. An environment variable that is set but does not parse as a number is a startup failure, named and fatal, not a shrug.

If you are writing a config loader, the three cases are distinct and only two of them are the same:

unset          -> use the default    (fine, intentional)
set + parses   -> use the value      (fine)
set + garbage  -> REFUSE             (never silently default)

The generalisation: "fall back to the default on error" is the correct policy for an absent value and the wrong policy for a malformed one. The user who set the variable told you they wanted something other than the default; giving them the default anyway contradicts an explicit instruction while looking like it obeyed.

A fourth, about method rather than configuration

There is now a test asserting that no page-level stylesheet redefines a class that the shared stylesheet defines.

That collision has bitten twice. Most recently the gallery defined .label — reasonably, for a gallery label — and .label is also what the block renderer calls a field label. Every input inside a preview rendered uppercase and tiny. Both times the cause was found by eye, staring at a page until something looked wrong.

Finding it by eye is not a method. It does not scale past the pages you happen to look at, it fails on the pages you look at while tired, and it gives no warning at the moment the collision is introduced — only later, when someone notices something looks off and has no reason to connect it to a CSS class name.

Worth stating explicitly, because it is the part that generalises furthest: the guard is proved to bite before it is trusted. A test written for a bug you have already fixed must be shown to fail against the bug. Reintroduce the collision, watch the test go red, remove it, watch it go green. A guard that has never failed is a guard you are only assuming works, and the whole reason for writing it was that assumption had already cost you twice.

Three deployment-facing bugs and one testing habit, recorded from a single commit. Written for the next person to self-host and hit them.

brief.rendered:
Three things self-hosting exposed

Running the project somewhere other than the original host surfaced three defects that had been invisible on the deployment that wrote them. Each announced itself with a symptom that pointed confidently at the wrong subsystem: an auth failure that was really an address failure, a shell command that was really a template-literal escape, and a config default that was really a parser giving up in silence. All three are fixed. The write-up is here because the misdirection is the expensive part, not the fix.

  • `unauthorized` on every call was the client talking to the wrong host, not signing badly.
  • A joined-up `claude mcp add` command was a line continuation eaten by a template literal, not a broken renderer.
  • MAX_AWAIT_MS=90s becoming 90 seconds was an unparseable value falling back to a default without saying so.
  • A fourth item — a CSS class collision — got a test rather than a fix, because it had already been found by eye twice.

Symptom, where it points, where it actually was

SymptomWhat it reads asActual cause
`unauthorized` on every MCP call from a freshly installed clientA broken or mismatched signature; key handling; clock skewThe client had this deployment's URL hardcoded as its default base URL, so it signed correct requests and sent them to somebody else's host, which had never seen the key
The `claude mcp add` command on /start arrives as one long joined lineA markdown or code-block renderer dropping newlinesA lone trailing backslash inside a template literal is a line continuation, not a backslash — the source lines were joined and the continuation character silently eaten before rendering ever happened
MAX_AWAIT_MS=90s behaves as 90 seconds; awaits time out early or lateA unit-parsing feature that exists and is being appliedThe value failed to parse as a number and the loader fell back to its default without reporting it, in a loader whose whole stated posture is refusing loudly

In each row, the symptom was truthful and the inference from it was wrong. That is the pattern worth remembering more than any of the three fixes.

The three, in detail

The MCP client hardcoded one deployment as its default base URL
A self-hoster who followed /start by hand installed a client whose default base URL was this deployment, not theirs. The client then signed requests with their key and sent them to a host that had never issued that key. Every call returned `unauthorized`, which reads as a signature problem, so the natural next move is to inspect key derivation, canonicalisation and clock skew — all of which are fine. The address was wrong. Fixed by having the instance substitute its own URL into the client file as it serves it, the way /cli already worked: a client downloaded from your deployment now talks to your deployment.
A trailing backslash inside a template literal is a line continuation
The multi-line `claude mcp add` command on /start was written in a JavaScript template literal with shell line continuations at the end of each line. In a template literal, a lone trailing backslash continues the source line: the newline and the backslash both disappear before the string exists. The rendered page therefore showed one joined line, with no trace of the continuation, and the page renderer — the obvious suspect — was innocent. Escape the backslash (`\\`) or build the command from an array and join it.
An unparseable numeric env var fell back to its default in silence
`MAX_AWAIT_MS=90s` looks like it means ninety seconds. It parsed to nothing, the loader substituted the default, and the process started normally. The behaviour that follows is a timeout that is neither what you configured nor obviously wrong — the worst kind, because the config file and the running system disagree with no evidence anywhere. This is in a loader whose stated posture is to refuse loudly rather than guess. It refuses now: an unparseable numeric value is a startup failure, not a shrug.
Fourth item: a stylesheet collision, fixed with a test rather than an eye
The gallery page defined `.label`, which is also what the shared block renderer calls a field label. Every input inside a preview rendered uppercase and tiny. This class of bug has bitten twice and both times was caught by somebody noticing it, which is not a method. There is now a test that no page stylesheet redefines a class the shared stylesheet defines. It was proved to fail against the collision before being trusted — a guard that has never been seen to bite is an assertion about a guard, not a guard.

The two that are easiest to reproduce

The continuation bug. Inside a template literal, the backslash at the end of each line is consumed by JavaScript, not passed through to the reader as shell syntax. What the page shows is one line, and the backslashes are gone.

// Wrong: the newlines and backslashes vanish before the string exists
const cmd = `claude mcp add sirdocalot \
  --transport http \
  ${baseUrl}/mcp`;

// Renders as:
//   claude mcp add sirdocalot   --transport http   https://example/mcp

// Right: escape the backslash, or don't use one
const cmd = [
  'claude mcp add sirdocalot \\',
  '  --transport http \\',
  `  ${baseUrl}/mcp`,
].join('\n');

The silent-default bug. The old shape returns the default for any value that fails to parse, including values that were plainly meant to configure something. The new shape distinguishes 'absent' from 'present and nonsense'.

// Before: MAX_AWAIT_MS=90s -> NaN -> default, silently
const n = Number(process.env[key]);
return Number.isFinite(n) ? n : fallback;

// After: absent is fine, unparseable is fatal
const raw = process.env[key];
if (raw === undefined || raw === '') return fallback;
const n = Number(raw);
if (!Number.isFinite(n)) {
  throw new Error(`${key}=${raw} is not a number (expected milliseconds)`);
}
return n;

What to verify on your own deployment

Client base URL
Open the MCP client file your instance serves and confirm the default base URL is your host, not the one you copied from. If it isn't, you downloaded a pre-fix client — fetch it again from your own deployment.
The /start command
The `claude mcp add` block should appear as multiple lines with visible trailing backslashes. One long line means you are on a pre-fix build; the command will still work if you paste it, but read it before trusting it.
Numeric environment variables
Values are milliseconds and must parse as bare numbers. `90s`, `1_000` and `90 ms` are now startup failures rather than silent defaults. If your instance suddenly refuses to boot after an upgrade, this is the likely reason and the error names the variable.
Page stylesheets
Do not define a class the shared stylesheet already defines — `.label` in particular. The test suite now fails on collisions rather than waiting for someone to notice tiny uppercase text.
The common thread: all three defects were invisible on the deployment that authored them, because that deployment was the hardcoded default, rendered its own /start page, and had a valid config file. Self-hosting is not only a feature here; it is the test environment that makes assumptions about 'the host' fail loudly enough to find.
brief.briefTitle: Three self-hosting bugs whose symptoms pointed somewhere other than their cause

artifact.output:
Three open questions in docs/DESIGN.md

The argument as it stands, and a position required from each maintainer on every open item.

Answers needed from: Priya and Sam. Nothing here is decided; the OPEN markers in the doc are reproduced faithfully.

1. The core bet: a schema, not a framework

The argument

Generating bespoke HTML costs thousands of output tokens every time, and that generation — not context loading, not deploy latency — is where the current approach is slow and expensive. So the agent-facing surface is a schema it emits against, not a framework it programs against:

{"type": "decision-matrix", "options": [...], "criteria": [...]}

That is a 20–50× token reduction over an authored page, and it is the entire reason this service exists. Any design decision that pushes agents back toward writing markup has broken the bet.

OPEN Worth confirming against two or three real past generations before committing. If the dominant cost turns out to be context loading rather than generation, the answer is a cached design doc, not this service.

What's at stake: if the cost model is wrong, the service has no reason to exist. The counter-position is that the 20–50× figure is self-evident enough to build on without measuring.

Priya — position
Sam — position

2. The per-dev cluster problem OPEN

The argument

Every dev runs their own independent single-node k3s cluster behind their own tunnel. So a participant link points at that dev's box. A stakeholder clicking it six hours later gets an answer only if that box is still up — and the box is also a NixOS host that gets rebuilt.

For a dev-phase tool this is probably tolerable: the boxes are always-on and the blast radius is one dev's briefs. It is not tolerable if links go to people outside the team, because a dead link to an external stakeholder is worse than never having sent one.

The cheap insurance, taken now: never bake the host into a brief's identity. A handle and a participant token identify a brief; the hostname serving it is deployment configuration. That costs nothing today and keeps "move it to one shared deployment" a config change rather than a migration.

What's at stake: this is named as the one risk worth raising up front. The open part is whether "tolerable for now, insured by indirection" is the right posture, or whether the shared deployment is owed sooner.

Priya — position

Is host-independent brief identity sufficient insurance?

Sam — position

Is host-independent brief identity sufficient insurance?

3. Agent-facing interface: MCP over the REST API

The argument

The REST API is built — see README.md for the routes. It is bearer-authenticated and is what the participant-facing app uses too.

OPEN An MCP server over the top, exposing list_widgets, create_brief, await_responses as tools. That is the idiomatic agent-facing surface and would remove the need for an agent to remember curl invocations. REST stays underneath either way, because an orchestrator resuming a session is not necessarily an agent.

What's at stake: only the timing and the scope. REST is not in question. The question is whether MCP is built now, deferred until REST has been exercised in anger, or skipped.

Priya — position
Sam — position

Anything the three questions miss

Priya
Sam
